title: Metals: Reactivity, Rusting and Extraction
description: The reactivity series with evidence from reactions with water, steam and dilute acid; rusting and its prevention by barrier methods; extraction methods matched to reactivity; the blast furnace and aluminium from bauxite — Core content for Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: The 0620 Reactivity Series
notes.body:
📌 The series you must know
**K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au** — potassium most reactive, gold least. Hydrogen is a non-metal marker included so you can predict acid reactions; carbon is another useful marker (it sits between Al and Zn) because it decides the extraction method.

🔑 How it works as an exam tool
• A metal's position predicts whether it reacts with water, steam or dilute acid, and how vigorously.
• The position also decides how the metal is extracted from its ore: electrolysis at the top, heating with carbon in the middle, found native at the bottom.
• Observations are the evidence: how fast a metal fizzes with acid, or glows in steam, places it in the series.

💡 Worked Example
Metal X fizzes steadily with dilute hydrochloric acid but does not react with cold water. X sits between the water-reactors (K-Ca) and hydrogen — e.g. magnesium, zinc or iron. Metal Y does not fizz at all: Y is below hydrogen, e.g. copper.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Quoting the KS3 series with lithium, tin and lead. The 0620 series is the one listed above — answers are marked against it.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Order: K Na Ca Mg Al | Zn Fe | H | Cu Ag Au.
• Above H: reacts with dilute acid. Below H: no reaction with dilute acid.

notes.heading: Reactions with Water and Steam
notes.body:
📌 The evidence ladder
• **K and Na** — react violently with cold water, skating on the surface; the hydrogen may ignite.
• **Ca** — reacts steadily with cold water, giving a cloudy solution of calcium hydroxide and bubbles of hydrogen.
• **Mg** — reacts only very slowly with cold water, but vigorously with **steam**, forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen.
• **Zn and Fe** — react with **steam** when red hot, forming the metal oxide and hydrogen (iron's reaction is reversible).
• **Cu, Ag, Au** — no reaction with water or steam.

🔑 The pattern
metal + cold water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen (only the most reactive metals)
metal + steam → metal oxide + hydrogen (the middle of the series, when heated)
The further down the series, the more violent conditions the metal needs — cold water at the top, red heat and steam in the middle, nothing works at the bottom.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that magnesium reacts vigorously with COLD water — it does not; that describes calcium. Magnesium needs steam. Note also the product difference: water gives the hydroxide, steam gives the oxide.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Cold water: K, Na (violent), Ca (steady), Mg (barely).
• Steam: Mg vigorously, Zn and Fe when red hot.
• Cu, Ag, Au: no reaction with either.

notes.heading: Reactions with Dilute Acids
notes.body:
📌 The rule
metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen — but ONLY for metals above hydrogen in the series: **Mg, Al, Zn, Fe** react; **Cu, Ag, Au** do not.

🔑 Using it as evidence
The vigour of the reaction mirrors the series: magnesium fizzes fastest, then aluminium (slow to start because of its oxide layer), then zinc, then iron — a gentle stream of bubbles. This is a classic 'place these metals in order' practical: the rate of bubbling is the evidence.

💡 Worked Example
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂: the zinc dissolves, bubbles form, and the gas gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint — the test for hydrogen.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Claiming copper reacts 'slowly' with dilute acid. Copper is below hydrogen, so there is NO reaction at all with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid — not a slow one. Also: never use these reactions with potassium or sodium — far too violent to do safely.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Vigour order with dilute acid: Mg > Al > Zn > Fe; Cu, Ag, Au: nothing.
• The gas is hydrogen — squeaky pop test.

notes.heading: Rusting and Barrier Methods
notes.body:
📌 The conditions
Rusting is the corrosion of iron (or steel) and it needs **BOTH oxygen AND water**. Take either away and rusting stops.

🔑 The proving experiments
• Nail in **dry air** (with a drying agent) → no rust: water is needed.
• Nail in **boiled water sealed under a layer of oil** → no rust: boiled water has no dissolved oxygen and the oil keeps air out — oxygen is needed.
• Nail half-dipped in **ordinary water open to the air** → rusts, fastest at the waterline where both oxygen and water are present.

📌 Prevention: barrier methods (Core)
Coating the iron so oxygen and water cannot reach it: **paint, oil or grease, and plastic coating**. The coating only works while it is intact — a scratch exposes the metal and rusting begins there.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying rusting needs 'air' — it needs the OXYGEN in air, plus water. 'Air and water' is accepted less reliably than 'oxygen and water'; use the gas name. (Coating methods that keep working when scratched, like galvanising, are Extended tier — not needed here.)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Rusting = iron + oxygen + water.
• Barrier methods: paint, oil/grease, plastic — all must stay unbroken.

notes.heading: Extraction Method Matches Reactivity
notes.body:
📌 The pattern
A metal's position in the reactivity series decides how it is extracted from its ore:
• **K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al** (above carbon): too reactive for carbon to reduce their oxides — extracted by **electrolysis** of molten compounds.
• **Zn, Fe** (below carbon): extracted by **heating the ore with carbon** — carbon takes the oxygen away.
• **Cu, Ag, Au**: so unreactive that some are found **native** (as the pure metal) — no chemical extraction needed.

🔑 Why carbon is the dividing line
Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc in the series. A metal below carbon 'wants' its oxygen less than carbon does, so heating with carbon reduces the ore: metal oxide + carbon → metal + carbon dioxide. Above carbon, the metal holds oxygen too strongly and only electricity can tear the compound apart.

💡 Worked Example
Predict the method for iron and for sodium: iron is below carbon → blast furnace (heating with carbon); sodium is above carbon → electrolysis.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying aluminium is extracted by heating with carbon 'because it is a metal'. Position, not metal-ness, decides: aluminium is above carbon, so carbon reduction fails and electrolysis is required.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Above carbon → electrolysis. Below carbon → heat with carbon. Very unreactive → native.
• The carbon marker is the dividing line.

notes.heading: The Blast Furnace: Extracting Iron
notes.body:
Iron ore is reduced in a blast furnace. At Core you describe the process in words (symbol equations are Extended).

📌 Raw materials (added at the top)
• **Iron ore** (haematite, iron(III) oxide) — the source of iron
• **Coke** (carbon) — the fuel and the source of the reducing agent
• **Limestone** (calcium carbonate) — to remove impurities
• **Hot air** — blasted in near the bottom

🔑 The three main stages
1. **Coke burns** in the hot air, forming carbon dioxide and releasing a great deal of heat — the furnace reaches over 1500 °C.
2. **The carbon dioxide reacts with more hot coke** to form carbon monoxide — the actual reducing agent.
3. **Carbon monoxide reduces the iron(III) oxide** to molten iron, which runs to the bottom of the furnace and is tapped off.

📌 Removing impurities
The limestone thermally decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with sandy impurities (silicon dioxide) to form **slag**. Slag floats on the molten iron and is tapped off separately.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'carbon reduces the iron oxide directly' as the main step, or crediting the limestone with producing iron. The reducing agent is carbon MONOXIDE; the limestone's job is slag formation only.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• In at the top: iron ore, coke, limestone. In at the bottom: hot air.
• Out: molten iron (bottom) and slag (floating above it).

illustration.alt: A labelled blast furnace: iron ore, coke and limestone enter at the top, hot air is blasted in near the bottom, carbon monoxide reduces the iron oxide to iron in the middle zone, and molten slag and molten iron are tapped off at the bottom.
illustration.caption: Coke burns to CO₂, CO₂ reacts with more coke to form CO, and CO reduces the iron oxide — limestone removes impurities as slag.

notes.heading: Aluminium: From Bauxite by Electrolysis
notes.body:
📌 The Core facts
• The main ore of aluminium is **bauxite**, which contains aluminium oxide (alumina, Al₂O₃).
• Aluminium is **too high in the reactivity series** for carbon reduction — it is above carbon — so it is extracted by **electrolysis** of molten aluminium oxide.

🔑 How it works (state-level)
The aluminium oxide must be molten so its ions can move and carry the current; electrolysis then splits it into aluminium (collected molten) and oxygen. The fine detail — cryolite, the electrodes, the half-equations — is Extended tier and is not required here.

💡 Why this matters economically
Electrolysis consumes huge amounts of electricity, which is why aluminium smelters sit near cheap power and why **recycling aluminium** saves about 95% of the energy of extracting it from bauxite.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Pairing the wrong ore or method: iron ← haematite ← blast furnace with carbon; aluminium ← bauxite ← electrolysis. Swapping 'bauxite' and 'haematite' is a classic lost mark.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bauxite is the ore; electrolysis is the method.
• Aluminium is above carbon, so heating with carbon cannot work.

flashcards.definition: K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe (H) Cu Ag Au — most to least reactive, with hydrogen as the marker for acid reactions.
flashcards.example: Magnesium is above hydrogen so it reacts with dilute acids; copper is below so it does not.

flashcards.definition: Only the most reactive metals react: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen. K and Na violently, Ca steadily.
flashcards.example: Calcium sinks in cold water giving a cloudy solution of Ca(OH)₂ and bubbles of H₂.

flashcards.definition: Middle-series metals react with steam when heated: metal + steam → metal oxide + hydrogen.
flashcards.example: Magnesium burns brightly in steam forming white MgO; red-hot iron and zinc also react.

flashcards.definition: Salt + hydrogen, only for metals above hydrogen (Mg, Al, Zn, Fe). Vigour decreases down the series.
flashcards.example: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂; copper, silver and gold do not react.

flashcards.definition: A lighted splint held at the gas gives a squeaky pop.
flashcards.example: The gas from zinc and dilute sulfuric acid pops with a lighted splint.

flashcards.definition: The corrosion of iron or steel, requiring BOTH oxygen and water together.
flashcards.example: A nail in dry air stays bright; a nail half-dipped in water open to the air rusts at the waterline.

flashcards.definition: Coatings that stop oxygen and water reaching the iron: paint, oil or grease, and plastic coating. They fail where scratched.
flashcards.example: Car bodies are painted; bicycle chains are oiled; garden furniture is plastic-coated.

flashcards.definition: Metals above carbon in the series (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds.
flashcards.example: Aluminium from molten aluminium oxide — carbon is not reactive enough to reduce it.

flashcards.definition: Metals below carbon (Zn, Fe) are extracted by heating the ore with carbon; the least reactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) occur native.
flashcards.example: Iron from haematite in the blast furnace; gold found as nuggets.

flashcards.definition: Iron ore (haematite), coke and limestone added at the top; hot air blasted in at the bottom.
flashcards.example: Products: molten iron tapped from the bottom and slag floating above it.

flashcards.term: Role of limestone in the blast furnace
flashcards.definition: Decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with sandy impurities (silicon dioxide) to form slag, which floats on the iron.
flashcards.example: Slag is tapped off separately and used in road building.

flashcards.definition: The main ore of aluminium; aluminium is extracted from it by electrolysis because aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series.
flashcards.example: Al₂O₃ must be molten for electrolysis; recycling aluminium saves ~95% of the extraction energy.

questions.stem: Which of these metals is the MOST reactive?
choices: Gold
Iron
Zinc
Potassium
questions.explanation: The 0620 series runs K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe (H) Cu Ag Au. Potassium tops the list; gold is at the unreactive bottom.

questions.stem: Which conditions are needed for iron to rust?
choices: Oxygen only
Oxygen and water together
Water only
Carbon dioxide and water
questions.explanation: Rusting needs both oxygen and water: a nail in dry air does not rust, and a nail in boiled water sealed under oil does not rust. Remove either condition and rusting stops.

questions.stem: Which of these metals reacts steadily with COLD water?
choices: Copper
Magnesium
Calcium
Gold
questions.explanation: Calcium reacts steadily with cold water, forming calcium hydroxide and hydrogen. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water (it needs steam to react vigorously); copper and gold do not react at all.

questions.stem: Zinc granules are added to dilute sulfuric acid. Which gas is produced?
choices: Hydrogen
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Sulfur dioxide
questions.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. The hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.stem: How is aluminium extracted from its ore?
choices: By electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide
By heating the ore with carbon
It is found native and needs no extraction
By heating the ore with limestone
questions.explanation: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce its oxide — electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (from bauxite) is required.

questions.stem: How is iron extracted from haematite?
choices: By electrolysis of molten iron ore
By digging out native iron
By heating the ore with carbon in a blast furnace
By dissolving the ore in acid
questions.explanation: Iron is below carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon (via carbon monoxide) can reduce iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace. Electrolysis is reserved for metals above carbon.

questions.stem: Which mixture of raw materials is added at the top of a blast furnace?
choices: Iron ore, limestone and sand
Iron ore, coke and chlorine
Bauxite, coke and limestone
Iron ore, coke and limestone
questions.explanation: The charge is iron ore (haematite), coke (carbon — fuel and source of the reducing agent) and limestone (to remove impurities as slag); hot air is blasted in near the bottom. Bauxite is the aluminium ore — not used here.

questions.stem: Which experiment provides the evidence that BOTH oxygen and water are needed for rusting?
choices: A nail in dry air rusts quickly
A nail in boiled water sealed under an oil layer does not rust, while a nail half-dipped in ordinary water open to the air does
A nail in pure oxygen rusts with no water present
A painted nail rusts faster than an unpainted nail
questions.explanation: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen from the water and the oil keeps air out, so that nail has water but no oxygen — and stays bright. The half-dipped control nail has both oxygen and water and rusts. Together with a dry-air nail (oxygen, no water — no rust), each condition is proved necessary.

questions.stem: What is formed when magnesium reacts with steam?
choices: Magnesium hydroxide and oxygen
No reaction — magnesium is unreactive
Magnesium oxide and hydrogen
Magnesium carbonate and water
questions.explanation: Metal + steam → metal oxide + hydrogen: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂. The hydroxide is the product with COLD water (for metals like calcium) — with steam the product is the oxide.

questions.stem: Gold is found native (as the pure metal) in the Earth's crust. What does this show about gold?
choices: Gold is so unreactive that it does not form compounds in nature, so it exists as the pure element
Gold is more reactive than iron
Gold is extracted by electrolysis
Gold ore is too deep to mine
questions.explanation: Only metals at the very bottom of the reactivity series (Ag, Au) are unreactive enough to exist uncombined over geological time. Reactive metals are always found as compounds (ores).

questions.stem: Which set lists only Core barrier methods of preventing rusting?
choices: Covering the iron with salt solution
Painting, oiling or greasing, and plastic coating
Drying the iron with a hairdryer every day
Bending the iron into a curved shape
questions.explanation: Barrier methods keep oxygen and water off the metal: paint, oil/grease and plastic coating. Salt solution actually speeds rusting, and the other options do not form a barrier.

questions.stem: Why can zinc be extracted by heating zinc oxide with carbon, while aluminium cannot?
choices: Zinc is above carbon in the reactivity series
Zinc oxide conducts electricity better than aluminium oxide
Carbon can reduce every metal oxide
Zinc is below carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon is reactive enough to take the oxygen from its oxide
questions.explanation: Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc in the series. It reduces the oxides of metals BELOW it (zinc, iron) but not those above it — aluminium holds its oxygen too strongly, so aluminium needs electrolysis.

questions.stem: Which metal is more reactive, magnesium or zinc — and what is the evidence?
choices: Zinc — it reacts faster with dilute acid
Magnesium — it is higher in the reactivity series and fizzes more vigorously with dilute acid
They are equally reactive because both react with acid
Zinc — because it is extracted by electrolysis
questions.explanation: Magnesium sits above zinc in the series, and the observation matches: magnesium fizzes more vigorously with dilute acid than zinc does. (Both are actually extracted differently too — but that is not the acid evidence.)

questions.stem: What is the role of limestone in the blast furnace?
choices: It provides the heat for the furnace
It reduces the iron(III) oxide to iron
It catalyses the burning of the coke
It decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with sandy impurities to form slag
questions.explanation: Limestone (calcium carbonate) decomposes in the heat to calcium oxide, a base that reacts with acidic silicon dioxide impurities to form molten slag. The reduction of the iron ore is done by carbon monoxide, not limestone.

questions.stem: Copper foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. Nothing happens. Why?
choices: Copper is above hydrogen in the reactivity series
The acid is too dilute to react with any metal
Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid
Copper reacts, but the gas produced is invisible
questions.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the series can displace hydrogen ions from an acid. Copper, silver and gold are below hydrogen, so there is no reaction with dilute acids at all.
